key_insight: MC-EvoBench shows that in embodied self-improvement, a successful outcome or saved memory is not enough to prove real learning. The benchmark is designed to separate true capability gains from shortcuts like carried-over resources, uneven task exposure, or one-off execution luck.
problem_solved: The paper addresses how to fairly evaluate whether Minecraft agents actually improve from experience in a way that transfers to new tasks and worlds, rather than just reusing prior resources or benefiting from confounding factors.
method: Introduces MC-EvoBench, a controlled Minecraft benchmark for auditing experience-driven self-improvement.
Uses evaluation setups that isolate capability change from confounders such as persistent resources, source-task exposure imbalance, and early failure effects.
Focuses on measuring whether learned behavior generalizes across worlds and later tasks, not just whether the agent completes a single episode successfully.
impact: This work gives researchers a more rigorous way to test recursive self-improvement in embodied AI. It can prevent misleading claims about learning and help practitioners build agents whose progress is real, transferable, and reproducible.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing experience -> memory -> capability -> transfer to new tasks.
A comparison chart contrasting true skill gain vs. confounded success from resources or exposure.
An icon-based benchmark schematic of multiple Minecraft worlds/tasks with controlled conditions.
A flowchart highlighting sources of evaluation bias and how MC-EvoBench controls them.
paper_title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
paper_authors: Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou
